Every edge is visited once, numbered in visit order on the accent arrows: 1 A to B, 2 B to C, and 3 C to A, which closes the cycle. The card lists the three edges beside bfs_edges, which keeps only the two tree edges (A, B) and (B, C)." width="100%"} Unlike `bfs_edges()`, which lists only the edges of the search tree, this visits *every* edge reachable from the source exactly once, including the ones that close cycles and each parallel edge. That makes it the right traversal for tasks about edges themselves: checking every link in reach, building an edge-indexed visit order, or finding cycles in directed graphs while respecting edge direction. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str, list, None]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : A start node, a list of start nodes, or `None` (default) for all nodes, in ID order. [orientation]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : How to treat direction on directed graphs: `None` (default) follows edges forward; `"original"` does the same but tags each edge `"forward"`; `"reverse"` follows edges backward (tagged `"reverse"`); `"ignore"` follows both ways and tags each edge with the direction it was traversed. Undirected graphs always traverse both ways. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The edges in visit order as `(u, v, edge_id)` triples (`u` being the node it was reached from on undirected graphs), with a fourth `"forward"`/`"reverse"` element when `orientation` is given. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a node does not exist or `orientation` is invalid. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A breadth-first search over nodes that emits each node's edges in turn, skipping edges already emitted (each edge ID once). $O(V + E)$. Matches NetworkX's `edge_bfs` on the corresponding (multi)graph, with edge IDs in place of keys. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A triangle's three edges are all visited, while `bfs_edges()` only gives the two tree edges: ::: {#ce09efb4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) [(g.get_label_from_id(u), g.get_label_from_id(v)) for u, v, _ in g.edge_bfs("A")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [('A', 'B'), ('B', 'C'), ('C', 'A')] ``` ::: :::
